Energy solution to Schrödinger-Poisson system in the two-dimensional whole space

Satoshi Masaki Address: Division of Mathematics
Graduate School of Information Sciences
Tohoku University
Sendai 980-8579, Japan Email address: masaki@ims.is.tohoku.ac.jp
Abstract.

We consider the Cauchy problem of the two-dimensional Schrödinger-Poisson system in the energy class. Though the Newtonian potential diverges at the spatial infinity in the logarithmic order, global well-posedness is proven in both defocusing and focusing cases. The key is a decomposition of the nonlinearity into a sum of the linear logarithmic potential and a good remainder, which enables us to apply the perturbation method. Our argument can be adapted to the one-dimensional problem.

1. Introduction

This paper is devoted to the study of the Schödinger-Poisson system

(1.1) {i∂tu+12Δu=λPu,(t,x)∈ℝ1+2,−Δ​P=|u|2,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}u+\frac{1}{2}\Delta u=\lambda Pu,\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{1+2},\\ &-\Delta P=|u|^{2},\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\end{aligned}\right.

where λ\lambda is a real constant. We suppose PP is the Newtonian potential

(1.2) P=−12​π​(log⁡|x|∗|u|2)P=-\frac{1}{2\pi}(\log|x|*|u|^{2})

where ∗* denotes the convolution. For a suitable uu, this is the unique strong solution of −Δ​P=|u|2-\Delta P=|u|^{2} under the condition

|∇P|→0​ as ​|x|→∞,∇P∈L∞​(ℝ2),P⁡(0)=∫ℝ2(log⁡|y|)​|u⁡(y)|2​𝑑y|\nabla P|\to 0\text{ as }|x|\to\infty,\quad\nabla P\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\quad P(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|y|)|u(y)|^{2}dy

(see [11]). When the dimensions are larger than two, the Schrödinger-Poisson system is a special case of the Hartree equation and one of the typical example of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a nonlocal nonlinearity, and there is large amount of literature (see [6] and references therein). On the other hand, the two-dimensional case is less studied. In [1, 18], (1.1) is considered with some restrictive assumptions such as a neutrality condition which confirms that the Newtonian potential (1.2) does not diverge at the spatial infinity and in particular belongs to L2L^{2} space. The Poisson equation is sometimes posed with a background (or doping profile):

−Δ​P=|u|2−b,-\Delta P=|u|^{2}-b,

where bb is a given positive function. Then, the neutrality condition is ∫|u|2−b​𝑑x=0\int|u|^{2}-bdx=0 or equivalently ℱ⁡(|u|2−b)​(0)=0\mathcal{F}(|u|^{2}-b)(0)=0. When we consider the problem in dimensions less than three, this condition is useful to control PP. Notice that this condition excludes all nontrivial solutions when b≡0b\equiv 0, and that we need to remove this condition for the study of (1.1). In [11], the above assumptions are removed and the existence of a unique local solution is proven for data in the usual Sobolev space Hs​(ℝ2)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (s>2)(s>2) despite the fact that the nonlinear potential diverges at the spatial infinity. Since (1.2) is not necessarily defined for u∈Hsu\in H^{s} (s>2s>2) we introduced a new formula

P=−12​π∫ℝ2(log|x−y||y|)|u(y)|2dyP=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{|y|}\right)|u(y)|^{2}dy

which makes sense merely if |u|2∈Lp​(ℝ2)|u|^{2}\in L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (p∈(1,2)p\in(1,2)). We underline that the local solutions given there do not have finite energy (the energy is given in (1.5) below). Our aim in this paper is to prove that there exists a time-global solution if initial data has finite energy.

For our analysis, the following reduction is crucial: We guess that the Newtonian potential (1.2) may behave like −12​π​‖u‖L22​log⁡|x|-\frac{1}{2\pi}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\log|x| at the spatial infinity, which will be the bad part of the nonlinearity, and decompose the nonlinearity as

λ​P​u=−λ2​π​‖u‖L22​(log⁡⟨x⟩)​u−λ2​π​u​∫ℝ2(log⁡|x−y|⟨x⟩)​|u⁡(y)|2​𝑑y,\lambda Pu=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}(\log\left\langle x\right\rangle)u-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}u\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}\right)|u(y)|^{2}dy,

where ⟨x⟩=(1+|x|2)1/2\left\langle x\right\rangle=(1+|x|^{2})^{1/2}. We then obtain

i∂tu+12Δu+λ2​π‖u‖L22(log⟨x⟩)u=−λ2​πu∫ℝ2(log|x−y|⟨x⟩)|u(y)|2dy.i{\partial}_{t}u+\frac{1}{2}\Delta u+\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}(\log\left\langle x\right\rangle)u=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}u\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}\right)|u(y)|^{2}dy.

It will turn out that the bad part of PP is correctly extracted from the original nonlinearity and therefore the behavior of the “new nonlinearity” becomes better. Notice that one can also expect that ‖u‖L2\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{2}} is conserved because λ\lambda is a real number. Hence, putting

m:=−λ2​π​‖u0‖L22,m:=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2},

we reach to the equation

(1.3) {i∂tu+(12Δ−mlog⟨x⟩)u=−λ2​πu∫ℝ2(log|x−y|⟨x⟩)|u(y)|2dy,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x).\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}u+\left(\frac{1}{2}\Delta-m\log\left\langle x\right\rangle\right)u=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}u\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}\right)|u(y)|^{2}dy,\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x).\end{aligned}\right.

Notice that −m​log⁡⟨x⟩-m\log\left\langle x\right\rangle is now completely independent of uu and that it therefore can be regarded as a linear potential. In what follows, we work with this equation. Observe that if there exists a solution to (1.3) conserving ‖u‖L2\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{2}}, then it is also a solution of (1.1).

Now, the linear part of the equation is not i∂t+(1/2)Δi{\partial}_{t}+(1/2)\Delta but i∂t+(1/2)Δ−mlog⟨x⟩i{\partial}_{t}+(1/2)\Delta-m\log\left\langle x\right\rangle. Thus, a natural choice of the function space on which we shall work is not the Sobolev space H1​(ℝ2)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) any more, but the following one:

(1.4) ℋ:={u∈H1​(ℝ2);log⁡⟨x⟩​u∈L2},\displaystyle\mathcal{H}:=\{u\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2});\sqrt{\log\left\langle x\right\rangle}u\in L^{2}\},
‖u‖ℋ:=‖u‖H1​(ℝ2)+‖log⁡⟨⋅⟩​u‖L2​(ℝ2).\displaystyle\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}:=\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}+\left\lVert\sqrt{\log\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle}u\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}.

If m>0m>0, that is, if λ<0\lambda<0, then the above space coincides with the form domain of the positive operator −12​Δ+m​log⁡⟨x⟩-\frac{1}{2}\Delta+m\log\left\langle x\right\rangle. Our main result is the following:

Theorem 1.1.

The problem (1.3) is globally well-posed in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Moreover, the solution conserves ‖u⁡(t)‖L2\left\lVert u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}} and the energy

(1.5) E⁡(t)=12​‖∇u​(t)‖L22−λ4​π​∫ℝ2(log⁡|x−y|)​|u⁡(t,x)|2​|u⁡(t,y)|2​𝑑x​𝑑y.E(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|x-y|)|u(t,x)|^{2}|u(t,y)|^{2}dxdy.
Corollary 1.2.

The Problem (1.1) is globally well-posed in ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Remark 1.3.

Let u∈C⁡(ℝ,ℋ)u\in C(\mathbb{R};\mathcal{H}) be a solution of (1.3) (and of (1.1)) given in Theorem 1.1. Then, v:=uexp(−iλ2​π∫0t∥log|⋅|u(s)∥L22ds)v:=u\exp(-i\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{t}\|\sqrt{\log|\cdot|}u(s)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}ds) solves

(1.6) {i∂tv+12Δv=−λ2​πv∫ℝ2(log|x−y||y|)|v(y)|2dy,v⁡(0,x)=u0​(x).\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}v+\frac{1}{2}\Delta v=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}v\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\log\frac{|x-y|}{|y|}\right)|v(y)|^{2}dy,\\ &v(0,x)=u_{0}(x).\end{aligned}\right.

Notice that the nonlinearity of (1.6) makes sense without the momentum condition log|⋅|​v∈L2\sqrt{\log|\cdot|}v\in L^{2}. This observation explains why existence of a time-local solution can be proven by assuming only u0∈Hs​(ℝ2)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (s>1s>1) in [11].

1.1. Consequent results

Our argument is also applicable to (1.1) involving a power type nonlinearity:

(1.7) {i∂tu+12Δu=λPu+η|u|p−1u,(t,x)∈ℝ1+2,−Δ​P=|u|2,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}u+\frac{1}{2}\Delta u=\lambda Pu+\eta|u|^{p-1}u,\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{1+2},\\ &-\Delta P=|u|^{2},\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\end{aligned}\right.

where η\eta is a real number and p⩾2p\geqslant 2.

Theorem 1.4.

The problem (1.7) is globally well-posed in ℋ\mathcal{H} if either one of the following conditions is satisfied:

  1. (1)

    η⩾0\eta\geqslant 0, λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} and p⩾2p\geqslant 2;

  2. (2)

    η<0\eta<0, λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, and 2⩽p<32\leqslant p<3;

  3. (3)

    η<0\eta<0, λ>0\lambda>0, p=3p=3, and ‖u0‖ℋ\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}} is small;

  4. (4)

    η<0\eta<0, λ<0\lambda<0, p⩾3p\geqslant 3, and ‖u0‖ℋ\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}} is small.

Moreover, the solution conserves ‖u⁡(t)‖L2\left\lVert u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}} and the energy

(1.8) Ep​(t):=\displaystyle E_{p}(t):={} 12​‖∇u​(t)‖L22−λ4​π​∫ℝ2(log⁡|x−y|)​|u⁡(t,x)|2​|u⁡(t,y)|2​𝑑x​𝑑y\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|x-y|)|u(t,x)|^{2}|u(t,y)|^{2}dxdy
+ηp+1​‖u⁡(t)‖Lp+1p+1.\displaystyle}{\displaystyle+\frac{\eta}{p+1}\left\lVert u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}.

The proof is done with a straight-forward modification (see Section 4). The case where p=3p=3 is known as the L2L^{2}-critical case. Since the ℋ\mathcal{H}-norm contains derivative, it seems difficult to treat the case 1<p<21<p<2. Nevertheless, we can show global well-posed in a slightly smaller function space ℋ1,2:={u∈H1​(ℝ2);u​log⁡⟨x⟩∈L2}\mathcal{H}^{1,2}:=\{u\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2});u\log\left\langle x\right\rangle\in L^{2}\}.

Theorem 1.5.

Suppose 1<p<21<p<2. For η,λ∈ℝ\eta,\lambda\in\mathbb{R} The problem (1.7) is globally well-posed in the space ℋ1,2\mathcal{H}^{1,2}. Moreover, the solution conserves ‖u⁡(t)‖L2\left\lVert u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}} and the energy Ep​(t)E_{p}(t) given in (1.8).

We can also handle the one-dimensional problem

(1.9) {i∂tu+12∂x​xu=−λ2(|x|∗|u|2)u+η|u|p−1u,(t,x)∈ℝ1+1,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}u+\frac{1}{2}{\partial}_{xx}u=-\frac{\lambda}{2}(|x|*|u|^{2})u+\eta|u|^{p-1}u,\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{1+1},\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\end{aligned}\right.

where λ,η∈ℝ\lambda,\eta\in\mathbb{R} and p⩾2p\geqslant 2. The one dimensional problem was studied in [7, 14, 15]. The global well-posedness of (1.9) was shown in the space {f∈H1​(ℝ);|x|​f∈L2​(ℝ)}\{f\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R});|x|f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\} in [15], and in the space {f∈H1​(ℝ);|x|​f∈L2​(ℝ)}\{f\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R});\sqrt{|x|}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\} with a presence of background in [7], provided λ>0\lambda>0 and data is small relative to the background. We can prove the global well-posedness result of (1.9) including these results.

Theorem 1.6.

The problem (1.9) is globally well-posed in {f∈H1​(ℝ);|x|​f∈L2​(ℝ)}\{f\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R});\sqrt{|x|}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\} if λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} and either one of the following conditions is satisfied:

  1. (1)

    η⩾0\eta\geqslant 0, λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, and p⩾2p\geqslant 2;

  2. (2)

    η<0\eta<0, λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, and 2⩽p<52\leqslant p<5;

  3. (3)

    η<0\eta<0, λ>0\lambda>0, p=5p=5, and ‖u0‖H1+‖|⋅|​u0‖L2\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{H^{1}}+\|{\sqrt{|\cdot|}u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}} is small;

  4. (4)

    η<0\eta<0, λ<0\lambda<0, p⩾5p\geqslant 5, and ‖u0‖H1+‖|⋅|​u0‖L2\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{H^{1}}+\|{\sqrt{|\cdot|}u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}} is small.

The solution conserves ‖u‖L2\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{2}} and the energy

(1.10) E~​(t):=12​‖∂xu‖L2​(ℝ)2−λ2​∬ℝ2|x−y|​|u⁡(x)|2​|u⁡(y)|2​𝑑x​𝑑y+ηp+1​‖u‖Lp+1​(ℝ)p+1.\widetilde{E}(t):=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\partial}_{x}u\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{2}\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|x-y||u(x)|^{2}|u(y)|^{2}dxdy+\frac{\eta}{p+1}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{L^{p+1}(\mathbb{R})}^{p+1}.

The one-dimensional version of Theorem 1.5 is as follows, which reproduce the same result in [15, Theorem 2.1] when η<0\eta<0 and λ>0\lambda>0.

Theorem 1.7.

Suppose 1<p<21<p<2. For η,λ∈ℝ\eta,\lambda\in\mathbb{R} The problem (1.9) is globally well-posed in the space Σ:={u∈H1​(ℝ2);|x|​u∈L2}\Sigma:=\{u\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2});|x|u\in L^{2}\}. Moreover, the solution conserves ‖u⁡(t)‖L2\left\lVert u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}} and the energy E~​(t)\widetilde{E}(t) given in (1.10).

As in the two dimensional case, the key is a “reduction” of (1.9) to

{i∂tu+12∂x​xu+λ​‖u0‖L222|x|u=−λ2u∫ℝ(|x−y|−|x|)|u(y)|2dy+η|u|p−1u,u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x).\left\{\begin{aligned} &i{\partial}_{t}u+\frac{1}{2}{\partial}_{xx}u+\frac{\lambda\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}}{2}|x|u=-\frac{\lambda}{2}u\int_{\mathbb{R}}{(|x-y|-|x|)}|u(y)|^{2}dy+\eta|u|^{p-1}u,\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x).\end{aligned}\right.

We briefly mention about other related works. Oh considered in [12] the Cauchy problem of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with general potential and L2L^{2}-subcritical power-type nonlinearity, and proved global well-posedness in the form domain of −12​Δ+V-\frac{1}{2}\Delta+V, provided the potential V⩾0V\geqslant 0 satisfies ∂αV∈L∞{\partial}^{\alpha}V\in L^{\infty} for |α|⩾2|\alpha|\geqslant 2 (see also [6]). In particular, the case where the potential VV is a quadratic polynomial is extensively studied. In this case, we have several special properties such as explicit representations of linear solutions, called Mehler’s formula, and/or of the Heisenberg observables. We refer the reader to [2, 3, 4, 10, 19] for H1H^{1}-subcritical and H1H^{1}-critical power-type nonlinearity and to [5] for H1H^{1}-subcritical Hartree type nonlinearity. In [16], the ground states of (1.1) is treated.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: We collect some basic estimates in Section 2, and, in Section 3 we prove Theorem 1.1. Section 4 is devoted to the study of (1.7).

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Strichartz estimate

We first summarize the properties on the operator

(2.1) A:=12​Δ−m​log⁡⟨x⟩,A:=\frac{1}{2}\Delta-m\log\left\langle x\right\rangle,

where m≠0m\neq 0 is a real constant. For any mm, AA is essentially self-adjoint on C0∞​(ℝ2)C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (see [13]). Since our potential is sub-quadratic, that is, since |∂αlog⁡⟨x⟩|→0|{\partial}^{\alpha}\log\left\langle x\right\rangle|\to 0 as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty for |α|=2|\alpha|=2 and ∂αlog⁡⟨x⟩∈L∞{\partial}^{\alpha}\log\left\langle x\right\rangle\in L^{\infty} for |α|⩾3|\alpha|\geqslant 3, the following estimate is established in [17]: For any T>0T>0,

‖ei​t​A​φ‖L∞⩽C​|t|−1​‖φ‖L1\left\lVert e^{itA}\varphi\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}}\leqslant C|t|^{-1}\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert_{L^{1}}

for t∈[−T,T]t\in[-T,T], where CC depends on TT (see also [8]). Once we know this type of estimate, the Strichartz estimate follows by interpolation. We say that a pair (q,r)(q,r) is admissible if 2⩽r<∞2\leqslant r<\infty and 2/q=δ⁡(r):=1−2/r2/q=\delta(r):=1-2/r.

Lemma 2.1 (Strichartz’s estimate).

For any T>0T>0, the following properties hold:

  • •

    Suppose φ∈L2​(ℝ2)\varphi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). For any admissible pair (q,r)(q,r), there exists a constant C=C⁡(T,q,r)C=C(T,q,r) such that

    ‖ei​t​A​φ‖Lq​((−T,T),Lr)⩽C​‖φ‖L2.\left\lVert e^{itA}\varphi\right\rVert_{L^{q}((-T,T);L^{r})}\leqslant C\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert_{L^{2}}.
  • •

    Let I⊂(−T,T)I\subset(-T,T) be an interval and t0∈I¯t_{0}\in\overline{I}. For any admissible pairs (q,r)(q,r) and (γ,ρ)(\gamma,\rho), there exists a constant C=C⁡(t,q,r,γ,ρ)C=C(t,q,r,\gamma,\rho) such that

    ‖∫t0tei⁡(t−s)​A​F​(s)​𝑑s‖Lq​(I,Lr)⩽C​‖F‖Lγ′​(I,Lρ′)\left\lVert\int_{t_{0}}^{t}e^{i(t-s)A}F(s)ds\right\rVert_{L^{q}(I;L^{r})}\leqslant C\left\lVert F\right\rVert_{L^{\gamma^{\prime}}(I;L^{\rho^{\prime}})}

    for every F∈Lγ′​(I,Lρ′)F\in L^{\gamma^{\prime}}(I;L^{\rho^{\prime}}).

2.2. Some estiamtes

Lemma 2.2.

Let WW be an arbitrary weight function such that ∇W\nabla W, Δ​W∈L∞​(ℝ2)\Delta W\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). It holds for all T>0T>0, admissible pair (q,r)(q,r), and φ∈ℋ\varphi\in\mathcal{H} that

‖[∇,ei​t​A]​φ‖Lq​((−T,T),Lr)⩽\displaystyle\left\lVert[\nabla,e^{itA}]\varphi\right\rVert_{L^{q}((-T,T);L^{r})}\leqslant{} C​|T|​‖φ‖2,\displaystyle C|T|\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert_{2},
‖[W,ei​t​A]​φ‖Lq​((−T,T),Lr)⩽\displaystyle\left\lVert[W,e^{itA}]\varphi\right\rVert_{L^{q}((-T,T);L^{r})}\leqslant{} C​|T|​‖(1+∇)​φ‖2.\displaystyle C|T|\left\lVert(1+\nabla)\varphi\right\rVert_{2}.
Proof.

Since v=ei​t​A​φv=e^{itA}\varphi solves i​∂tv+A​v=0i{\partial}_{t}v+Av=0, an explicit calculation shows

[∇,ei​t​A]φ=−i∫0tei⁡(t−s)​Am​x1+x2ei​s​Aφds[\nabla,e^{itA}]\varphi=-i\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(t-s)A}\frac{mx}{1+x^{2}}e^{isA}\varphi ds

and

[W,ei​t​A]φ=i∫0tei⁡(t−s)​A(∇W⋅∇+12ΔW)ei​s​Aφds.[W,e^{itA}]\varphi=i\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(t-s)A}\left(\nabla W\cdot\nabla+\frac{1}{2}\Delta W\right)e^{isA}\varphi ds.

The Strichartz estimate therefore gives the desired estimates. ∎

The following is useful for estimates of the nonlinearity in (1.3).

Lemma 2.3.

Set a function

K⁡(x,y)=log⁡|x−y|⟨x⟩1+log⁡⟨y⟩K(x,y)=\frac{\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}}{1+\log\left\langle y\right\rangle}

of x,y∈ℝ2x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. For any p∈[1,∞)p\in[1,\infty) and ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exist a function W⁡(x,y)⩾0W(x,y)\geqslant 0 with ‖W‖Ly∞​Lxp⩽ε\left\lVert W\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}_{y}L^{p}_{x}}\leqslant\varepsilon and a constant C0C_{0} such that

|K⁡(x,y)|⩽C0+W⁡(x,y)|K(x,y)|\leqslant C_{0}+W(x,y)

holds for all (x,y)∈ℝ2+2(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2+2}.

Proof.

Take η∈(0,1]\eta\in(0,1] and set W⁡(x,y)=|K⁡(x,y)|​𝟏|x−y|⩽η​(x,y)W(x,y)=|K(x,y)|{\bf 1}_{|x-y|\leqslant\eta}(x,y). If η\eta is sufficiently small then

‖W⁡(⋅,y)‖Lp⩽‖log⁡|x|‖Lp​(|x|⩽η)+log⁡⟨|y|+η⟩​‖1‖Lp​(|x|⩽η)1+log⁡⟨y⟩⩽ε\left\lVert W(\cdot,y)\right\rVert_{L^{p}}\leqslant\frac{\left\lVert\log|x|\right\rVert_{L^{p}(|x|\leqslant\eta)}+\log\left\langle|y|+\eta\right\rangle\left\lVert 1\right\rVert_{L^{p}(|x|\leqslant\eta)}}{1+\log\left\langle y\right\rangle}\leqslant\varepsilon

3.2. Global existence

We first give a useful blow-up criteria.

Lemma 3.2.

Suppose u0∈ℋu_{0}\in\mathcal{H}. Let u∈C⁡((−Tmin,Tmax),ℋ)u\in C((-T_{\mathrm{min}},T_{\mathrm{max}});\mathcal{H}) be a unique maximal solution given by Lemma 3.1. Since TT is arbitrary, we obtain the global existence. ∎

4. Remarks on the problem with power nonlinearity

We give a rough sketch of the proofs of Theorem 1.4 and 1.5 in this section.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

The local well-posedness part holds if p⩾2p\geqslant 2 as in the proof of Lemma 3.1. The restriction p⩾2p\geqslant 2 is required when we estimate

|∇(|u1|p−1​u1−|u2|p−1​u2)|⩽Cp​(|u1|p−2+|u2|p−2)​(|∇u1|+|∇u2|)​|u1−u2|+Cp​(|u1|p−1+|u2|p−1)​|∇(u1−u2)|.|\nabla(|u_{1}|^{p-1}u_{1}-|u_{2}|^{p-1}u_{2})|\leqslant C_{p}(|u_{1}|^{p-2}+|u_{2}|^{p-2})(|\nabla u_{1}|+|\nabla u_{2}|)|u_{1}-u_{2}|\\ +C_{p}(|u_{1}|^{p-1}+|u_{2}|^{p-1})|\nabla(u_{1}-u_{2})|.

By exactly the same argument as in Lemma 3.2, the problem of global existence boils down to obtaining an a priori bound of ‖∇u​(t)‖L2\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}. Recall that the conserved energy is

Ep​(t):=\displaystyle E_{p}(t):={} 12​‖∇u​(t)‖L22−λ4​π​∫ℝ2(log⁡|x−y|)​|u⁡(t,x)|2​|u⁡(t,y)|2​𝑑x​𝑑y\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|x-y|)|u(t,x)|^{2}|u(t,y)|^{2}dxdy
+ηp+1​‖u⁡(t)‖Lp+1p+1.\displaystyle{}+\frac{\eta}{p+1}\left\lVert u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}.

The case η>0\eta>0

We have

‖∇u​(t)‖L22⩽Ep​(t)+λ4​π​∫ℝ2(log⁡|x−y|)​|u⁡(t,x)|2​|u⁡(t,y)|2​𝑑x​𝑑y.\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\leqslant E_{p}(t)+\frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(\log|x-y|)|u(t,x)|^{2}|u(t,y)|^{2}dxdy.

By the same argument as in the case η=0\eta=0, we prove global existence.

The case η<0\eta<0 and λ<0\lambda<0

Since

|η|p+1​‖u⁡(t)‖Lp+1p+1⩽Cη,p​‖u0‖L22​‖∇u​(t)‖L2p−1,\frac{|\eta|}{p+1}\left\lVert u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\leqslant C_{\eta,p}\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{p-1},

we obtain

‖∇u​(t)‖L22⩽2​E0+C​‖∇u​(t)‖L2+2​Cη,p​‖u0‖L22​‖∇u​(t)‖L2p−1\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\leqslant 2E_{0}+C\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+2C_{\eta,p}\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{p-1}

as in (3.6). Uniform bound of ‖∇u​(t)‖L2\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}} is then obtained either the case p<3p<3 or the case p⩾3p\geqslant 3 and ‖u0‖L2\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{2}} is small.

The case η<0\eta<0 and λ>0\lambda>0

As in (3.7), for any T>0T>0, there exist ε\varepsilon, C1C_{1}, and C2C_{2} such that

(sups∈[0,t]‖∇u​(s)‖L2)2⩽\displaystyle\left(\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left\lVert\nabla u(s)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}\right)^{2}\leqslant{} 4​E​(0)+4​C1+4​C2​(ε+2​T)​sups∈[0,t]‖∇u​(s)‖L2\displaystyle 4E(0)+4C_{1}+4C_{2}(\varepsilon+2T)\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left\lVert\nabla u(s)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}
+4​Cη,p​‖u0‖L22​(sups∈[0,t]‖∇u​(s)‖L2)p−1.\displaystyle{}+4C_{\eta,p}\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\left(\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left\lVert\nabla u(s)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}\right)^{p-1}.

for t⩽2​Tt\leqslant 2T. Therefore, if p<3p<3 or if p=3p=3 and ‖u0‖L2\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{L^{2}} is small, we obtain

supt∈[0,2​T]‖∇u​(t)‖L2⩽C⁡(‖u0‖ℋ,T)<∞.\sup_{t\in[0,2T]}\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}\leqslant C(\left\lVert u_{0}\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}},T)<\infty.

This concludes the proof of Theorem 1.4. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

We denote Lp​((−T,T),X)=LTp​XL^{p}((-T,T);X)=L^{p}_{T}X. Our strategy for local well-posedness is to use the contraction argument in a complete metric space (ℋT,M1,2,d)(\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T,M},d), where

ℋT,M1,2:={f∈C⁡((−T,T),H1);‖f‖ℋT1,2⩽M},\displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T,M}:=\{f\in C((-T,T);H^{1});\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T}}\leqslant M\},
‖f‖ℋT1,2:=‖f‖LT∞​ℋ+‖f‖LTq0​W1,r0+‖f​log⁡⟨x⟩‖LTq0​Lr0\displaystyle\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T}}:=\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{H}}+\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L^{q_{0}}_{T}W^{1,r_{0}}}+\left\lVert f{\log\left\langle x\right\rangle}\right\rVert_{L^{q_{0}}_{T}L^{r_{0}}}

for an admissible pair (q0,r0)(q_{0},r_{0}) with r0>2r_{0}>2, and the metric dd is given by

(4.1) d⁡(f,g)=‖f−g‖LT∞​L2+‖f−g‖LTq0​Lr0.d(f,g)=\left\lVert f-g\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{2}}+\left\lVert f-g\right\rVert_{L^{q_{0}}_{T}L^{r_{0}}}.

We shall show

Q⁡[u]​(t,x):=(ei​t​A​u0)​(x)+i2​π​(∫0tei⁡(t−s)​A​(∫ℝ2log⁡|⋅−y|⟨⋅⟩​|u⁡(s,y)|2​dy)​u​(s,⋅)​ds)​(x)−i​η​(∫0tei⁡(t−s)​A​(|u|p−1​u)​(s)​ds)​(x)Q[u](t,x):=(e^{itA}u_{0})(x)\\ +\frac{i}{2\pi}\left(\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(t-s)A}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\log\frac{|\cdot-y|}{\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle}|u(s,y)|^{2}dy\right)u(s,\cdot)ds\right)(x)\\ -i\eta\left(\int_{0}^{t}e^{i(t-s)A}(|u|^{p-1}u)(s)ds\right)(x)

is a contraction map in (ℋT,M1,2,d)(\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T,M},d). Mimicking the proof of Lemma 3.1, one shows that for any M>0M>0, there exists T>0T>0 such that Q:ℋT,M1,2→ℋT,M1,2Q:\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T,M}\to\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T,M}. To prove QQ is a contraction with respect to the metric dd, the following estimate is crucial:

‖(∫ℝ2log⁡|x−y|⟨x⟩​|u1​(y)|2​𝑑y)​u1−(∫ℝ2log⁡|x−y|⟨x⟩​|u2​(y)|2​𝑑y)​u2‖L2\displaystyle\left\lVert\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}|u_{1}(y)|^{2}dy\right)u_{1}-\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}|u_{2}(y)|^{2}dy\right)u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}
⩽‖(∫ℝ2log⁡|x−y|⟨x⟩​|u1​(y)|2​𝑑y)​(u1−u2)‖L2\displaystyle{}\leqslant\left\lVert\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}|u_{1}(y)|^{2}dy\right)(u_{1}-u_{2})\right\rVert_{L^{2}}
+‖(∫ℝ2log⁡|x−y|⟨x⟩​(|u1​(y)|2−|u2​(y)|2)​𝑑y)​u2‖L2\displaystyle\quad+\left\lVert\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\log\frac{|x-y|}{\left\langle x\right\rangle}(|u_{1}(y)|^{2}-|u_{2}(y)|^{2})dy\right)u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}
⩽C⁡(‖u1‖L22+‖log⁡⟨x⟩​u1‖L22)​(‖u1−u2‖L2+‖u1−u2‖Lr0)\displaystyle{}\leqslant C(\left\lVert u_{1}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\sqrt{\log\left\langle x\right\rangle}u_{1}\|_{L^{2}}^{2})(\left\lVert u_{1}-u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+\left\lVert u_{1}-u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{r_{0}}})
+C⁡(‖|u1|2−|u2|2‖L1+‖(|u1|2−|u2|2)​log⁡⟨x⟩‖L1)​(‖u2‖L2+‖u2‖Lr0)\displaystyle\quad+C(\left\lVert|u_{1}|^{2}-|u_{2}|^{2}\right\rVert_{L^{1}}+\|(|u_{1}|^{2}-|u_{2}|^{2})\log\left\langle x\right\rangle\|_{L^{1}})(\left\lVert u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+\left\lVert u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{r_{0}}})
⩽C⁡(‖u1‖L22+‖log⁡⟨x⟩​u1‖L22)​(‖u1−u2‖L2+‖u1−u2‖Lr0)\displaystyle{}\leqslant C(\left\lVert u_{1}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\sqrt{\log\left\langle x\right\rangle}u_{1}\|_{L^{2}}^{2})(\left\lVert u_{1}-u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+\left\lVert u_{1}-u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{r_{0}}})
+C⁡(‖u1‖L2+‖u2‖L2+‖u1​log⁡⟨x⟩‖L2+‖u2​log⁡⟨x⟩‖L2)\displaystyle\quad+C(\left\lVert u_{1}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+\left\lVert u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+\|u_{1}\log\left\langle x\right\rangle\|_{L^{2}}+\|u_{2}\log\left\langle x\right\rangle\|_{L^{2}})
×(‖u2‖L2+‖u2‖Lr0)​‖u1−u2‖L2.\displaystyle\quad\quad\times(\left\lVert u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+\left\lVert u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{r_{0}}})\left\lVert u_{1}-u_{2}\right\rVert_{L^{2}}.

By the Strichartz estimate, letting TT smaller if necessary, we hence obtain

d⁡(Q⁡[u1],Q⁡[u2])⩽12​d​(u1,u2)d(Q[u_{1}],Q[u_{2}])\leqslant\frac{1}{2}d(u_{1},u_{2})

for any u1,u2∈ℋT,M1,2u_{1},u_{2}\in\mathcal{H}^{1,2}_{T,M}.

A similar result as Lemma 3.2 holds since

|dd​t‖log⟨x⟩u(t)‖L22|=|Im∫2​x​log⁡⟨x⟩1+x2⋅∇u(t)u⁡(t)¯dx|⩽C‖∇u(t)‖L2.\left\lvert\frac{d}{dt}\left\lVert\log\left\langle x\right\rangle u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}^{2}\right\rvert=\left\lvert\operatorname{Im}\int\frac{2x\log\left\langle x\right\rangle}{1+x^{2}}\cdot\nabla u(t)\overline{u(t)}dx\right\rvert\leqslant C\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}.

Now, we have a priori bound of ‖∇u​(t)‖L2\left\lVert\nabla u(t)\right\rVert_{L^{2}} as in the case 2⩽p<32\leqslant p<3 of Theorem 1.4, which proves the global well-posedness. ∎
